Hackers start exploiting critical WordPress flaw for code execution

In plain words

Hackers are actively using a serious weakness in WordPress, software used to run websites, to place files on vulnerable sites that can run commands when opened. The issue affects WordPress sites that have not installed the new security update, with some common PHP and hosting setups increasing the risk. This matters because an outsider may be able to take control of a website, so site owners should update WordPress quickly and check for suspicious activity.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting the critical WordPress path-traversal flaw CVE-2026-87902 to write PHP files and potentially execute shell commands on vulnerable sites. Administrators should urgently update to WordPress 7.1.2 or a supported backported release and review logs for malicious requests.

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-87902, a critical WordPress flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to write files to disk and potentially execute shell commands. Patchstack observed initial reconnaissance activity less than five hours after WordPress released a patch, and related traffic later increased tenfold. Some payloads merely mark a site as exploitable, while others create files that execute a shell command when accessed.

The flaw is a path traversal issue in WordPress page-template resolution that can include a chosen readable local PHP file outside the active theme directories. Remote code execution requires specific conditions, including a theme directory whose name starts with “page-” and a readable local PHP file; the advisory identifies pearcmd.php as an example in certain PHP configurations. WordPress fixed the issue in version 7.1.2 and backported fixes to branches down to 4.7, while versions before 4.6 will not receive a fix. Administrators are advised to update promptly and review logs for malicious requests, including double-encoded traversal sequences in the pagename parameter used with a valid page_id.

  • Attackers progressed from identifying vulnerable WordPress sites to attempting file writes within a day, and Patchstack recorded a tenfold increase in related traffic.
  • Remote command execution depends on specific conditions, including a theme directory beginning with "page-" and a readable local PHP file; the article identifies pearcmd.php as a possible target in affected PHP configurations.
  • Observed payloads use pearcmd's config-create function to write attacker-controlled files to /tmp or /var/tmp, including files designed to execute a shell command when accessed.
  • The malicious probes use double-encoded directory-traversal sequences in the pagename parameter together with a valid page_id, providing a specific log-review indicator.
Key Points
  • 01Threat actors are actively exploiting the critical WordPress flaw CVE-2026-87902 to write files that can execute shell commands when accessed.
  • 02CVE-2026-87902 is an unauthenticated path traversal issue that can lead to remote code execution under certain conditions, and WordPress assigned it a critical severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
  • 03Patchstack observed reconnaissance requests less than five hours after the WordPress 7.1.2 patch was released, followed by a tenfold increase in traffic and payloads intended to write files to disk.
  • 04WordPress fixed the flaw in version 7.1.2 and backported fixes to supported branches down to version 4.7, while releases before 4.6 will not receive a fix.
  • 05Administrators should update WordPress promptly and review logs for malicious activity, including requests using double-encoded traversal sequences in the pagename parameter alongside a valid page_id.

In plain words

Check Point says hackers are actively using two security weaknesses in its network-security products to get into customer systems before logging in. The affected customers include users of Check Point Security Gateway, Spark firewalls, and the company’s management service. This matters because attackers can use these openings to run their own software on a target’s systems, while hiding where they are coming from, so customers should install the available fixes or limit who can connect.

Summary
Check Point confirmed active exploitation of two pre-authentication flaws, CVE-2026-85102 in Security Gateway VPN certificate handling and CVE-2026-93616 in its Management web service. Organizations should immediately apply the specified LivePatch or hotfix updates and restrict VPN access if patching is not possible.

Check Point has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-85102, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw in the VPN certificate-handling functionality of its Security Gateway product. The company also warned about CVE-2026-93616, a pre-authentication path traversal flaw in its Management web service that can allow script execution and Java class loading. Check Point says CVE-2026-93616 has been exploited as a zero-day since July 23, while exploitation attempts against Spark customers involving CVE-2026-85102 began on September 12.

Check Point observed the attempts coming from anonymization infrastructure, including VPN services and proxies, and identified several certificate subjects used in current activity. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and told U.S. federal agencies to apply fixes or mitigations by September 25, 2026. Check Point recommends LivePatch Take 26 or specified fixed hotfix versions for supported Security Gateway releases, plus updated Spark firewall builds; where updates cannot be installed, it advises restricting VPN access with explicit network rules, although those mitigations do not apply to locally managed Spark firewalls.

  • Organizations that previously installed an earlier offline LivePatch package may still lack full protection unless they install LivePatch Take 26.
  • The temporary network-rule mitigation does not apply to locally managed Spark firewalls, making software updates especially important for those deployments.
  • The certificate subjects observed in attacks are useful for investigation, but Check Point cautions that they represent only current observations and attackers may use additional subjects.
  • The two actively exploited issues affect different entry points: Security Gateway VPN certificate handling and the Management web service, so addressing only one does not cover both risks.
Key Points
  • 01Check Point confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-85102, a flaw in Security Gateway VPN certificate handling that can let an attacker run code before logging in.
  • 02The company also warned that CVE-2026-93616, affecting its Management web service, has been exploited as a previously unknown flaw since July 23 and can enable script execution and Java class loading.
  • 03Check Point observed exploitation attempts against Spark customers beginning September 12, 2026, originating from anonymization infrastructure including VPN services and proxies.
  • 04CISA added both CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-93616 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and directed U.S. federal agencies to apply fixes or mitigations by September 25, 2026.
  • 05Check Point recommends installing LivePatch Take 26 or the applicable fixed Jumbo Hotfix for supported Security Gateway versions, and updating Spark firewalls to the specified fixed releases.

    In plain words

    F5 released fixes for a serious flaw in its BIG-IP Access Policy Manager software that attackers are already using to run commands on affected systems from afar. The risk applies to organizations using this software as the part of their login system that authorizes access, while setups using it only to connect to other authorization services are not affected. U.S. federal agencies have been told to fix the issue by Friday, and the problem matters because F5 products are widely used by major companies and have repeatedly been targeted to gain access to networks and steal or destroy data.

    Summary
    F5 patched CVE-2026-94127, a critical BIG-IP Access Policy Manager flaw that is actively being exploited for remote code execution on deployments configured as OAuth authorization servers. Organizations should apply the updates immediately or use F5’s iRule mitigation and check for compromise indicators.

    F5 released security updates for CVE-2026-94127, a critical zero-day flaw in BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) that has been exploited in remote code execution attacks. The issue affects BIG-IP APM instances configured as OAuth Authorization Servers when both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile are configured on a virtual server. Deployments that use APM only as an OAuth Client or Resource Server, without OAuth authorization-server profiles, are not affected.

    F5 advises customers to investigate for possible compromise when multiple OAuth authentication failures and suspicious commands are followed shortly by a TMM SIGABRT. Organizations unable to install the updates immediately can apply an F5-provided iRule to the affected virtual server as a mitigation. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure affected networks by Friday; Shadowserver tracks more than 14,700 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints, although that number may include patched devices and honeypots.

    • A practical sign of possible compromise is a sequence of multiple OAuth authentication failures and suspicious commands followed shortly by a TMM SIGABRT crash.
    • The affected population is narrower than all BIG-IP APM users: risk depends on the specific combination of an OAuth authorization-server profile and an APM access policy on a virtual server.
    • Shadowserver identifies more than 14,700 internet-facing IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints, although the article notes that this total may include patched systems and honeypots.
    • Organizations unable to patch immediately can apply an F5-provided iRule to the affected virtual server as a temporary mitigation.

    Is This A Joke? In The Auth Header? (F5 BIG-IP UnAuth Heap-Overflow to RCE CVE-2026-94127)
    labs.watchtowr.com · 23 Sep 2026 23:19 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSbig-ipbig-ip-apmcve-2026-94127f5heap-overflowicontrol-restret2pltselinuxstack-pivotingtmostmuiunited-states
    In plain words

    Researchers examined a flaw in F5 BIG-IP APM, a widely used system that sits at the edge of company networks and helps direct web traffic and manage sign-ins. On affected versions, an attacker can send an overly long sign-in-related request without logging in, causing the device to crash and potentially take control of it. This matters because these devices can handle encrypted traffic and authentication for many applications, so a compromise could give an attacker a powerful position inside an organization’s network.

    Summary
    watchTowr Labs found that CVE-2026-94127 is an unauthenticated heap overflow in F5 BIG-IP APM OAuth endpoints, triggered by an oversized Authorization header and potentially enabling remote code execution. Affected BIG-IP APM deployments should apply F5’s hotfixes immediately.

    watchTowr Labs analyzed CVE-2026-94127, a flaw in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) OAuth functionality. F5’s advisory lists BIG-IP APM 21.1.0 and specified 17.x versions as affected, with hotfixes available for those branches. The issue is notable because BIG-IP devices can sit at the edge of a network, handling traffic, TLS termination, and authentication-related functions.

    The researchers found that vulnerable code allocated a fixed 0x4100-byte heap buffer and copied an Authorization header value into it without checking its size first. The patch adds a check that rejects Authorization headers larger than 0x4100 bytes, and the researchers triggered a crash on an unpatched OAuth-configured system by sending an oversized Bearer Authorization header to an OAuth endpoint. They reported that, in many test runs, the overflow could overwrite a nearby callback function pointer; although SELinux blocked a direct shell launch, they described using a crash-triggered script to run a command.

    • The flaw is confined in F5’s advisory to BIG-IP APM, even though BIG-IP’s other modules and BIG-IQ Centralized Management are listed as not affected.
    • The vulnerable code allocated a fixed 0x4100-byte buffer and copied the Authorization header into it without first checking the header’s length, while the fix was a direct size check.
    • The article’s proof of concept required an OAuth profile to be configured and an OAuth endpoint to be reachable, making that configuration relevant to exposure.
    • System-wide address randomization and non-executable heap and stack protections were enabled, but the main BIG-IP binary was not built as a position-independent executable.
    • SELinux prevented the researchers from directly launching a shell, but they found that modifying the script run after the traffic-management process crashes could still execute a command.
    Key Points
    • 01CVE-2026-94127 affects F5 BIG-IP APM OAuth functionality in BIG-IP APM 21.1.0 and selected 17.x releases, while F5 lists hotfixes for the affected branches.
    • 02The patched code rejects Authorization header values larger than 0x4100 bytes before copying them into a heap buffer of the same size.
    • 03On an unpatched system with an OAuth profile configured, sending an Authorization header larger than 0x4100 bytes to an OAuth endpoint caused the target process to crash.
    • 04The researchers reported that a heap object containing a callback function pointer landed after the overflowing buffer in roughly 90% of their test runs, allowing the function pointer to be overwritten.
    • 05Although SELinux blocked an attempted shell launch, the researchers described appending a command to the /etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish crash hook script as a way to run a command after the target process crashed.

BIG-IP devices commonly handle edge traffic, TLS termination, and authentication functions, making the affected deployments especially consequential.

In plain words

F5 says attackers are already using a serious flaw in certain BIG-IP systems to take control of them without needing a username or password. It affects organizations that use the BIG-IP Access Policy Manager to issue login access tokens for apps, rather than systems using it only to connect to or check those tokens. This matters because these systems help control access to company applications and networks, so a takeover could give attackers a foothold in important infrastructure; F5 has released fixes and a temporary workaround.

Summary
F5 has issued emergency hotfixes for CVE-2026-94127, a critical actively exploited BIG-IP APM flaw that enables unauthenticated remote code execution when APM is configured as an OAuth authorization server. Organizations should apply the branch-specific hotfix or F5’s temporary iRule mitigation immediately and investigate affected systems for compromise indicators.

F5 has disclosed and patched CVE-2026-94127, a critical heap-based buffer overflow in BIG-IP Access Policy Manager that attackers are actively exploiting for remote code execution without authentication. The issue affects deployments where APM acts as an OAuth authorization server, issuing access tokens, and where an APM access policy and OAuth authorization-server profile are configured on the same virtual server. F5 rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 under CVSS v3.1, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 22.

Restricting the BIG-IP management interface does not protect against the flaw because malicious traffic is sent to the OAuth-facing virtual server; systems in Appliance mode are also vulnerable. F5 released engineering hotfixes for affected BIG-IP 17.1, 17.5, and 21.1 branches, and offers an iRule mitigation through support when patching cannot happen immediately. Organizations should also check for repeated invalid OAuth token requests, suspicious audit-log commands, and TMM crashes, while recognizing that F5 has not stated whether the hotfix removes any attacker access already established.

  • Restricting access to the BIG-IP management interface does not mitigate this issue because the malicious traffic is sent to the OAuth-facing virtual server, and Appliance mode systems are also vulnerable.
  • The affected condition is narrower than some early advisories indicated: F5 says only APM deployments acting as OAuth authorization servers are affected, while APM OAuth clients and resource servers without authorization-server profiles are not.
  • Organizations already running fixes for the earlier APM issue CVE-2025-53521 may still be exposed, because the relevant 17.1 and 17.5 fixed builds remain within the affected ranges for CVE-2026-94127.
  • F5’s reported compromise pattern is a sequence rather than a single signal: repeated invalid-token UserInfo failures, suspicious audit-log commands, and then a TMM SIGABRT shortly afterward should prompt human review.
  • F5 did not assess BIG-IP versions that have reached End of Technical Support, so those versions should be treated as having an unknown status rather than as unaffected.
Key Points
  • 01F5 reports that CVE-2026-94127 is being actively exploited and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on affected BIG-IP Access Policy Manager systems.
  • 02The flaw affects BIG-IP deployments where Access Policy Manager acts as an OAuth authorization server and has an access policy and authorization-server profile on the same virtual server.
  • 03F5 rates the heap-based buffer overflow at 9.8 out of 10 under CVSS v3.1 and has released engineering hotfixes for BIG-IP 17.1, 17.5, and 21.1.
  • 04CISA added CVE-2026-94127 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and directed U.S. federal civilian agencies to apply mitigations by September 25.
  • 05F5 advises using a branch-specific hotfix or, when that cannot be installed immediately, an iRule mitigation available through F5 support.

MikroTrick Chain Let Attackers Take Over MikroTik Routers Without a Password or SSH Key
thehackernews.com · 23 Sep 2026 16:06 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSargument-injectioncert-polskacisacve-2026-67276cve-2026-67279cve-2026-86060mikrotikmikrotrickpolandrouterosssh-key-renegotiation

In plain words

Attackers have been using two linked flaws in MikroTik routers to take complete control of devices that can be reached from the public internet, without needing a password or key. The problem affects organizations and people who configured these routers to allow remote access through SSH, a common method for managing a device from elsewhere. Someone who takes over a router can create their own administrator account and may copy configuration data, so owners should install MikroTik’s updates and check whether their devices were altered before the fix.

Summary
CERT Polska says attackers are actively chaining two MikroTik RouterOS SSH flaws, CVE-2026-67279 and CVE-2026-86060, to gain full administrator access to Internet-exposed routers without credentials. Administrators should urgently update RouterOS, restrict public SSH access, and investigate devices for indicators such as failed logins using the username "-2" or unauthorized "ops" accounts.

CERT Polska’s technical analysis identifies the MikroTrick attack chain as two MikroTik RouterOS SSH flaws, CVE-2026-67279 and CVE-2026-86060. When chained, they allow attackers to take full administrative control of Internet-exposed routers without a password, SSH key, or completed authentication. Evidence in logs indicates the chain was exploited before MikroTik released patches on September 3. MikroTik fixed the flaws in RouterOS versions 6.49.21, 7.23.4, and 7.24.2.

The first flaw lets an unauthenticated SSH client reach the command stage by forcing key renegotiation during login, while the second makes the RouterOS login program treat the username “-2” as an option. This enables the attacker to supply a chosen username and a full-administrator privilege level through the SSH session, opening a privileged console. CERT Polska cited indicators including failed SSH logins for “-2,” unauthorized “ops” administrator accounts, and activity involving IP addresses 82.192.72.4 and 103.102.31.18. Patching stops the attack but does not remove prior changes, so administrators who find indicators should isolate and reset affected devices, rebuild from a trusted configuration, and change credentials.

  • Updating RouterOS prevents further use of the chain but does not undo accounts, configuration changes, or data theft that may have occurred before patching.
  • The RouterOS Flagged status can detect only selected signs of compromise, so a device not marked as flagged cannot be assumed to be clean.
  • A failed SSH login for the unusual username "-2" is a particularly useful investigation clue because it reflects the argument-handling behavior used in the observed attack chain.
  • The two flaws have complementary roles: one bypasses the normal point at which SSH verifies identity, while the other turns access to the login process into a fully privileged console.
  • The risk is concentrated on devices whose SSH service is reachable from untrusted public networks; MikroTik says its default home configuration does not expose SSH to the internet.
Key Points
  • 01CERT Polska’s MikroTrick analysis describes a chain of CVE-2026-67279 and CVE-2026-86060 that can give an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control of an Internet-exposed MikroTik RouterOS device over SSH.
  • 02CVE-2026-67279 lets a client reach the SSH command stage by triggering key renegotiation during authentication, while CVE-2026-86060 allows the username "-2" to be interpreted by the RouterOS login program as an option that reads identity and privilege data from the session terminal.
  • 03MikroTik released patches in RouterOS versions 6.49.21, 7.23.4, and 7.24.2, but CERT Polska found evidence that the chain was exploited before those fixes were available.
  • 04Observed indicators include SSH login attempts using the username "-2," creation of a fully privileged "ops" account, and activity involving IP addresses 82.192.72.4 and 103.102.31.18.
  • 05CERT Polska recommends that administrators finding compromise indicators isolate the router, preserve logs and configuration, factory reset and rebuild it from a trusted configuration, and change all passwords and keys.

In plain words

Arista Networks released fixes for a serious flaw in its VeloCloud Orchestrator management system that is already being abused by attackers. Organizations that run this system on their own computers are affected, especially if it is reachable through the web. An attacker may be able to reach sensitive internal controls without needing an account, which could let them change or disrupt how an organization’s network connections are managed. U.S. civilian federal agencies have been directed to secure affected systems by September 25.

Summary
Arista Networks has patched CVE-2026-93952, a maximum-severity VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day actively exploited to access privileged internal VCO functionality without tenant credentials. Administrators should patch immediately, restrict VCO web access, and investigate logs and indicators tied to the known malicious IP addresses.

Arista Networks released security patches for CVE-2026-93952, a maximum-severity zero-day affecting on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments that is known to be actively exploited. The flaw is caused by improper input validation and affects setups using certificate-based authentication between VeloCloud Edge and VeloCloud Orchestrator. Arista said an attacker can access privileged internal VCO host functionality through a low-complexity attack without target-system privileges, user interaction, or VCO tenant or operator credentials.

A successful attack requires network access to the VCO web interface and access to the public portion of a VeloCloud Edge authentication certificate. Arista has already patched hosted deployments on VCO 5.2.3.16 or later and 6.4.2.8 or later, and plans fixes for instances running 6.1.3.7 and below and 7.0.0.2 and below. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered U.S. federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected networks by September 25. Arista advised administrators to limit VCO web access to administrative networks, review logs and administrator activity, block two listed IP addresses, and preserve relevant logs if compromise is suspected.

  • The exposure does not require VCO tenant or operator credentials, but it does require network access to the VCO web interface and the public portion of a VeloCloud Edge authentication certificate.
  • Arista specifically recommends restricting VCO web-interface access to administrative networks while patches are deployed, indicating that limiting web exposure is an immediate mitigation step.
  • Defenders can look for the x-vc-opt HTTP header in nginx logs, encoded characters or unusual path components in web requests, and outbound HTTP or HTTPS connections from the VCO host.
  • Arista has patched two other actively exploited zero-day flaws affecting EOS and on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments since the start of the year.
Key Points
  • 01Arista Networks released patches for CVE-2026-93952, a maximum-severity VeloCloud Orchestrator On-Prem flaw that is known to be actively exploited.
  • 02The flaw affects deployments where certificate-based authentication is configured between VeloCloud Edge devices and VeloCloud Orchestrator.
  • 03An attacker with network access to the VCO web interface and the public portion of an Edge authentication certificate can access privileged internal VCO host functionality without tenant or operator credentials.
  • 04Arista said hosted deployments running VCO 5.2.3.16 or later and VCO 6.4.2.8 or later have already been patched, with fixes planned for other affected versions.
  • 05CISA added CVE-2026-93952 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and directed U.S. federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected systems by September 25.

In plain words

A financially motivated criminal used AI-powered tools to break into online stores, place hidden code that steals payment details, and take more than 600,000 valid credit card records. At least 119 websites were affected, including sites linked to large U.S. companies, so shoppers and retailers could both face fraud, lost data, and business disruption. The attackers reportedly spent only a few dollars to a few dozen dollars per target, showing how AI can help one person carry out many harmful break-ins quickly and cheaply.

Summary
A financially motivated actor used open-source AI agents to autonomously scan, compromise, and implant payment skimmers on at least 119 retail websites, stealing over 600,000 credit card records. The campaign shows how AI-driven automation can enable high-volume attacks at a very low per-target cost.

A financially motivated threat actor has used open-source AI agent frameworks to target online retailers at scale since at least July. Gambit reported that the campaign was still active on September 22 and that, between September 10 and 15, the attacker launched 105 attack waves with varying success against at least 27 companies. The operation used Strix for scanning and finding weaknesses, Cairn to seek access such as a shell or administrator privileges, and Hermes to coordinate activity and make tactical decisions using Claude Opus 4.6.

Gambit found that more than 600,000 valid card records were stolen from two companies and that payment-stealing code was deployed on at least 119 websites. The code was inserted by modifying legitimate JavaScript, checkout pages, Google tag blocks, S3/CDN content, caches, database fields, Kubernetes deployments, and scheduled tasks that could restore the code after removal. The attacker also instructed Hermes to erase card data from Magento databases after taking it, causing data loss and operational disruption at some retailers. Gambit estimated total operating costs of roughly \(12,000 to \)18,000, or an average of about $25 per target.

  • The attacker’s AI agent was instructed to erase stolen card data from Magento databases after downloading it, which created operational disruption and data loss for some retailers beyond the payment-card theft itself.
  • The campaign used multiple ways to insert and preserve payment-stealing code, including altering cloud-hosted content, databases, Kubernetes deployments, and scheduled tasks that reinstalled the code after removal.
  • The human operator reportedly provided only short goal-oriented instructions while the AI agents conducted much of the scanning, access attempts, and follow-on activity autonomously.
  • Gambit’s cost findings indicate that the operation could target companies for as little as $3.13 per completed scan, with a reported average of $25.46 across 101 scans.

  • 02The campaign was active from at least July through September 22 and launched 105 distinct attack waves between September 10 and 15, affecting at least 27 companies to varying degrees.

  • 04The attackers inserted payment-stealing code through methods including modified JavaScript files and checkout pages, poisoned S3/CDN content and server-side caches, altered database fields and Kubernetes deployments, and cron jobs that restored removed code.
  • 05Gambit estimated the operation cost roughly $12,000 to $18,000 in total, with the operator calculating a mean cost of $25.46 across 101 completed scans.

    In plain words

    Next.js fixed a serious flaw that could let an attacker run commands on a website’s server by putting specially crafted text into an image-generation request. It affects apps using Next.js versions 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 that create social-preview images on the standard Node.js server setup and place user-controlled information into those images. Website owners should update to version 16.3.6 because successful misuse could give an attacker control over the server running the site.

    Summary
    Next.js 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 has a critical ImageResponse flaw (CVE-2026-94545) that can enable server-side code execution when attacker-controlled input reaches generated SVG content on the Node.js runtime. Developers should upgrade to Next.js 16.3.6 immediately and prevent untrusted values from entering SVG content, attributes, or styles.

    A critical vulnerability in Next.js ImageResponse, tracked as CVE-2026-94545, could allow attackers to run code on a server through specially crafted SVG-related input. It affects Next.js versions 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 when ImageResponse runs on the Node.js runtime, which is the default. The Edge version of ImageResponse and Next.js 15 are not affected.

    ImageResponse uses Vercel’s Satori library to turn image layouts into SVG before producing PNG social-preview images. Certain attacker-controlled values could reach Satori’s SVG output without proper escaping and be interpreted as SVG code rather than ordinary text, potentially reaching flaws in other unnamed dependencies and leading to code execution. Vercel fixed the issue in Next.js 16.3.6, while developers unable to upgrade are advised to keep untrusted values out of SVG content, attributes, and styles; as of September 23, no public exploitation or exploit code had been reported.

    • Standard dependency checks may miss this issue: npm audit did not flag the affected Next.js 16.3.5 version as of September 23, and the advisory was not yet in the GitHub Advisory Database or published as a CVE record.
    • The vulnerable Satori component is bundled inside Next.js, so checking a lockfile alone will not show it as a Next.js dependency; applications need to verify their installed Next.js version directly.
    • Vercel did not state whether applications hosted on its platform are protected, unlike its messaging for two critical Next.js flaws fixed in August.
    • The advisory provides no method to determine whether an affected image-generation route was abused before patching, and recommends keeping untrusted values out of SVG output if an upgrade must wait.
    Key Points
    • 01CVE-2026-94545 is a critical Next.js ImageResponse flaw that could allow server code execution when attacker-controlled values are included in generated SVG content, attributes, or styles.
    • 02The issue affects Next.js 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 when ImageResponse runs on the default Node.js runtime, while Next.js 15 and the Edge version of ImageResponse are not affected.
    • 03Vercel fixed the vulnerability in Next.js 16.3.6 and advises applications on the 16.2 line to upgrade to that version because no fixed 16.2 release was listed.
    • 04The underlying Satori issue allowed certain values to reach SVG output without proper escaping, so specially crafted input could be interpreted as SVG code rather than plain text.
    • 05As of September 23, The Hacker News found no public reports of active exploitation or public exploit code for the flaw.

In plain words

The article warns about a serious flaw in Next.js, software used to build many public websites, that can let a visitor run harmful commands on a website’s server through specially crafted social-media preview images. It affects sites using certain recent Next.js versions that create these images on their own servers and include information supplied by visitors, such as text from a web address or form. This matters because marketing sites, online stores, documentation sites, and campaign pages commonly use this feature, and their ownership and update status can be difficult for organizations to track. Updating to Next.js 16.3.6 and checking how these image pages handle visitor-supplied information are the recommended steps.

Summary
CVE-2026-94545 is a critical Next.js Node.js ImageResponse flaw that can enable remote code execution when attacker-controlled input is rendered into dynamic SVG-based Open Graph images. Organizations using Next.js 16.2–16.3 should upgrade to 16.3.6 and review public image routes for untrusted request data.

CVE-2026-94545 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Next.js’s next/og ImageResponse API. The Node.js implementation can incorrectly escape values during SVG generation, allowing attacker-influenced values in image content, attributes, or styles to be interpreted as SVG markup. Publicly reachable dynamic Open Graph image routes are a common potential exposure point because they often generate images from request parameters, form fields, or API requests.

The issue affects Next.js versions 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 when the Node.js implementation is used and untrusted data reaches generated SVG output; the Edge implementation is not affected. Next.js 16.3.6 contains the fix, while version 15.5.26 adds hardening for the 15 line, and there is no same-minor backport for 16.2.x. Organizations should inventory internet-facing Next.js sites, identify dynamic ImageResponse routes, trace request data into generated images, and monitor those routes for malformed or unusually long parameters.

  • External scans can identify Next.js services but generally cannot determine the deployed framework version, whether ImageResponse is used, or whether the route runs on Node.js, making exposure difficult to confirm from outside an organization.
  • Filtering suspicious input is not considered a reliable safeguard because the underlying issue is how values are inserted into SVG output rather than simply the contents of those values.
  • Organizations on Next.js 16.2.x cannot apply a same-version patch and must upgrade to 16.3.6, which may require planning for teams pinned to 16.2 for dependency reasons.
  • Potentially affected sites may be owned by marketing or digital teams and deployed through managed hosting, so they can fall outside conventional infrastructure patch-management processes.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-94545 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Next.js's Node.js next/og ImageResponse API, caused by inadequate escaping of values rendered into SVG output.
  • 02The issue affects Next.js versions 16.2.0 through 16.3.5 when a Node.js ImageResponse route places attacker-influenced data into generated SVG content, attributes, or styles; the Edge implementation is not affected.
  • 03Next.js 16.3.6 fixes the vulnerability, while Next.js 15.5.26 provides hardening for the 15.x line and no backport exists for 16.2.x.
  • 04Organizations should inventory internet-facing Next.js sites, identify dynamic ImageResponse routes, determine whether request data reaches generated SVG, and monitor image routes for malformed or unusually long parameters.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This advisory describes a critical remote code execution flaw in the widely used Next.js framework, with a fixed release available and potentially exposed public image-generation routes. Security professionals should prioritize identifying affected Node.js ImageResponse deployments and upgrading to Next.js 16.3.6.

    Malicious releases of MemTensor’s npm package @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin—versions 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25—and PyPI package MemoryOS==2.0.34 were published on September 23, 2026. The affected releases bundle cross-platform Go binaries named sckit that launch in the background and search developer home directories and environment variables for credentials. At the time of writing, npm 0.1.25 and PyPI 2.0.34 were the latest versions, so default installs could retrieve compromised builds.

    In the npm plugin, the payload runs when the OpenClaw gateway starts and again for each memory recall, receiving the user’s prompt text through SCKIT_EVENT_TEXT. In the PyPI package, importing memos is enough to start the payload because the altered logging setup triggers it during module initialization. The embedded configuration identifies skyleen[.]fr subdomains as command-and-control infrastructure and shows that the payload targets credentials for services including npm, PyPI, GitHub, GitLab, AWS, Vault, and SSH.

    The article advises treating any host that loaded the affected npm versions or imported MemoryOS==2.0.34 as compromised, including developer machines, CI runners, and test containers. Recommended actions include removing or pinning the packages to known-good versions, rotating secrets available to the affected account, killing sckit processes, deleting related cache directories, and reviewing network activity for connections to skyleen[.]fr. Organizations are also advised to review their own package releases if exposed machines held npm or PyPI publishing tokens.

    • The malicious npm releases were interleaved with versions 0.1.22 and 0.1.24 that matched the last known-good release except for version strings, while 0.1.25 was assigned the latest tag.
    • Affected PyPI users may have triggered the payload simply by importing the memos module, because widely used package logging code starts it during module initialization.
    • The npm payload was launched again for every memory recall and received the user’s prompt through an environment variable, making prompt content an additional exposure concern.
    • The compromised PyPI distribution included files aimed at MemTensor’s own publishing workflow, and the payload contains strings associated with package publishing, so the article specifically advises reviewing package releases made with tokens present on affected hosts.
    • The payload’s configuration includes an October 22, 2026 expiration date, but the article still directs organizations to investigate connections to the listed skyleen.fr servers beginning September 23, 2026.
    Key Points
    • 01Malicious releases of the npm package @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin versions 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25, along with PyPI package MemoryOS version 2.0.34, were published on September 23, 2026.

The program was designed to search a person’s home folder and the app’s available settings for passwords, access tokens, and other sensitive information, and it may also receive users’ AI prompts. Developers, companies, and automated build systems using the affected package versions could have exposed cloud, code-hosting, package-publishing, and other account access, so removing the software alone is not enough—those credentials may need to be changed.

    Summary
    Malicious releases of MemTensor’s OpenClaw npm plugin and MemoryOS 2.0.34 for PyPI bundled the Sckit payload, which can launch silently during normal use or import, inherit environment credentials, and scan home directories for secrets. Organizations should remove affected versions, investigate process and network activity, and promptly rotate potentially exposed package, cloud, source-control, and CI credentials.

    Malicious versions 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25 of the @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin npm package included a hidden Sckit executable. The plugin could launch the payload during gateway startup and memory recall, passing the host process environment and, for recall events, the user’s prompt text. The package contents briefly returned to clean versions twice before malicious artifacts reappeared minutes later, indicating that recovery must address unauthorized publishing access as well as affected installations.

    The bundled payload configuration identifies the user’s home directory as an inventory root, and static strings include patterns for cloud, source-control, package-registry, and other credentials. The article also directly analyzes MemoryOS 2.0.34, whose Python logging setup can reach a similar platform-specific launcher during a normal memos import. Organizations that ran affected versions are advised to contain impacted hosts or runners, rebuild from trusted artifacts, investigate process and network activity, and revoke potentially exposed credentials from a clean system.

    • The malicious npm package contents were briefly replaced with clean artifacts twice before payloads reappeared within about three and a half minutes, meaning remediation must include revoking unauthorized publishing access rather than only replacing the package version.
    • The npm payload does not rely on an installation-time script; it can launch later when the affected plugin starts or recalls memory, so installing with package scripts disabled does not prevent execution during subsequent use.
    • Version 0.1.25 added a bundled certificate authority file that is used only when Linux lacks a usable system certificate bundle, potentially making the payload’s encrypted network connections more reliable in minimal containers and CI environments.
    • Although the MemoryOS build backend includes a function that could modify the GitHub Actions environment, the supplied source does not call that function, so the article does not establish that builds or installations automatically activate the CI path.
    • If the conditional MemoryOS publishing bridge is sourced by its intended upload shell, its final "exit 0" would terminate that shell after the helper runs, potentially preventing the remaining upload commands from continuing.

In plain words

Unknown attackers altered two MemTensor software packages available through npm and PyPI, so that installing or using certain versions could secretly run a program called sckit on Windows, Linux, or macOS. The program searches developers’ computers and automated work jobs for passwords, access tokens, cloud credentials, and private keys, then sends them to an outside server. This matters because stolen access can let attackers enter source-code accounts, cloud services, and software publishing accounts, potentially allowing the compromise to spread into additional software packages.

Summary
Compromised MemTensor packages on npm and PyPI deployed the cross-platform sckit credential stealer, which targets developer and CI secrets including cloud, source-control, and package-publishing tokens. Users should downgrade to known-safe versions, rotate potentially exposed credentials, terminate sckit processes, and block skyleen.fr.

Unknown threat actors compromised legitimate MemTensor packages on npm and PyPI to distribute a cross-platform Go-based implant called sckit for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Affected releases include @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin versions 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25, plus MemoryOS version 2.0.34, which is quarantined on PyPI. The malicious npm versions launch the payload when the agent gateway starts and during memory-recall events, while the PyPI version launches it when the memos module is imported.

Sckit searches developer machines and CI jobs for credential files, sensitive environment variables, cloud access keys, source-code tokens, package-registry tokens, private keys, and other secrets, then sends the data to skyleen.fr. SafeDep said the attackers obtained publishing tokens from MemTensor GitHub Actions release pipelines and that the implant contains templates for spreading through npm packages, Python packages, and GitHub Actions workflows. Because malicious npm versions remained available when the article was published, affected users are advised to pin to version 0.1.20 for the npm package or 2.0.33 for the PyPI package, rotate exposed secrets, stop any sckit process, and block skyleen.fr and its subdomains.

  • The malicious npm releases were interspersed with clean versions: 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25 were compromised, while 0.1.22 and 0.1.24 were clean.
  • During memory-recall events, the npm plugin’s launcher passes both the host process environment and the user’s prompt text directly to the malicious executable.
  • The implant includes templates for placing itself in npm packages, Python packages, and GitHub Actions workflows, giving it the potential to propagate through developer and publishing environments.
  • Because the malicious npm versions remained available for download when the article was published, pinning to version 0.1.20 and rotating any exposed secrets are immediately actionable measures.

In plain words

Researchers released code showing that someone inside a software container on certain Ubuntu systems could break out and take full control of the underlying computer. Ubuntu versions 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 using affected Linux software, including some cloud-hosted systems, have not yet received a fix. This matters because containers are commonly used to keep untrusted programs separate, but this flaw can bypass that separation; the researchers say organizations should consider stronger isolation that gives each workload its own operating system core.

Summary
A public exploit for CVE-2026-80521 can let an attacker escape an Ubuntu container and gain root access on the host through a use-after-free flaw in the Linux kernel’s AF_UNIX socket subsystem. Ubuntu 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 systems using affected kernels remain unpatched, so organizations should update when fixes arrive or isolate untrusted workloads with microVMs.

DepthFirst published research and exploit code for CVE-2026-80521, a use-after-free flaw in the Linux kernel’s AF_UNIX socket subsystem that can let an attacker escape a container and gain root access on the host. The exploit targets Ubuntu 26.04, while Ubuntu 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 LTS releases remained unpatched at the time of reporting. Affected Ubuntu kernel packages include versions used on AWS, Azure, and GCP workloads. There are no confirmed reports of the flaw being used in attacks, and it is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The bug is in the kernel component that cleans up file descriptors passed between local processes through SCM_RIGHTS messages. A race condition can leave a pointer to freed memory in an internal list, allowing a later cleanup pass to follow it. Because AF_UNIX sockets and the necessary ordinary system calls are permitted by default in Docker and Kubernetes seccomp profiles, the exploit can bypass container namespaces, cgroup limits, and seccomp filtering. The upstream fix landed in mainline Linux kernel 7.2 and stable 7.1.10, but neither DepthFirst nor Ubuntu published a temporary workaround; DepthFirst recommends microVM isolation such as Firecracker or Kata Containers for untrusted workloads.

  • The issue is especially significant because it can be triggered through normal system calls that are permitted in default Docker and Kubernetes configurations, allowing it to bypass several common container isolation controls.
  • Affected Ubuntu kernel packages include variants used for AWS, Azure, and GCP workloads, extending the exposure beyond standard on-premises Ubuntu installations.
  • A public exploit targets Ubuntu 26.04, yet the article reports no confirmed in-the-wild attacks and says the flaw is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
  • DepthFirst said its AI-assisted vulnerability research found the flaw, while the kernel maintainers indicated that an OpenAI researcher independently reported the same issue.
  • Because no temporary workaround was published, DepthFirst recommends moving untrusted workloads to microVM-based isolation such as Firecracker or Kata Containers, which do not share the host kernel.

Summary
North Korea-linked attackers are expanding the Graphalgo supply-chain campaign to HashiCorp Terraform Registry and Go modules, using trojanized packages to deploy malware with Slack and blockchain-based command-and-control. The activity reinforces the risk of fake-job-interview lures and compromised developer ecosystems as routes into production environments.

Researchers at Aikido identified Go-based malware distributed through two Terraform providers in HashiCorp Registry and two Go modules. The packages, including gocommunity-io/dockerd and kreuzwenker/docker, share infrastructure with the Graphalgo campaign, which has been attributed to North Korean threat actors. The discovery marks the first reported use of HashiCorp’s centralized Terraform Registry to distribute malicious payloads. Aikido said the tactic may offer a more direct route to credentials used in critical production environments.

The malware collects system and hardware information, hostname, operating-system details, and Node.js availability before sending the data to an attacker-controlled Slack channel. It then creates temporary encryption keys and uses Slack plus an Ethereum smart contract on the Arbitrum Sepolia testnet to receive encrypted commands, which can run Go or JavaScript code. Related npm packages were also found using encrypted payloads, cryptographic conditions that trigger execution, blockchain-based communications, and Slack channels. The article also describes fake job-interview and coding-task lures used to involve developers with seemingly legitimate repositories containing malicious dependencies.

  • Some related npm packages activate only after a specific cryptographic calculation, which researchers described as evidence of a targeted operation and a way to hinder analysis without the matching front-end component.
  • Terraform providers are an especially consequential distribution route because Terraform can offer a direct path to credentials used for critical production environments.
  • The blockchain command system limits operators because every infected client receives all messages but only acts on messages it can decrypt, reducing the risk of commands or data being exposed between infected hosts.
  • The GHAPPIER loader remained available through npm for only 35 minutes and 38 seconds, yet similar code was found in 65 public repositories after attackers used developers’ stored credentials to write to repositories they could access.

In plain words

Investigators found that a partner of the INC ransomware group tricked a person into running a command on their computer, then moved through the organization’s network and tried to shut off its security software. The attackers used several trusted-but-flawed software components and disguised a backdoor as part of a well-known security product, allowing them to copy files and send data to cloud storage. This matters because ransomware groups are gaining ready-made tools that can more reliably disable protections, making it easier for them to steal data and disrupt organizations.

Summary
A Beazley investigation found an INC ransomware affiliate used a ClickFix infection to gain access, then deployed four BYOVD toolkits to disable endpoint defenses and a backdoor hidden in a modified SentinelOne DLL. The case signals that ransomware operators are increasingly operationalizing reusable EDR-killing tools and legitimate-software camouflage.

Beazley Security investigated an INC ransomware incident in which an affiliate gained access through a ClickFix-style trick that led a user to run a malicious PowerShell command. The actor then installed a Python implant identified as TWINLOOT, harvested credentials, attempted RDP logins, and used pass-the-hash activity to move through the network. The backdoor was used for interactive activity including downloading utilities, changing local firewall rules, and installing a Wasabi client for data exfiltration.

Investigators found four separate bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver packages deployed across multiple hosts, an unusual volume for a ransomware case according to Beazley. Three involved known drivers, while the novel Redacted EDR Blinder installed a vulnerable IoDrv driver and overwrote key functions in several endpoint-security products so they would immediately exit. The affiliate also concealed a backdoor in a modified SentinelOne DLL that retained much of the original file’s appearance but had its signature removed and an encrypted payload embedded in its resources. The incident illustrates how ransomware operators may increasingly use reusable tools to disable endpoint defenses and disguise malicious code as legitimate security-related software.

  • Beazley’s DFIR team reported that this was the first ransomware intrusion it had seen using four distinct vulnerable-driver toolkits across multiple hosts, rather than the more typical single toolkit.
  • The Redacted EDR Blinder included a polished help interface for criminal users, which the article says suggests it was designed as a reusable, commoditized tool rather than for one intrusion.
  • The modified SentinelOne library retained the original icon and metadata but had its digital signature removed, showing that superficial file characteristics can still resemble legitimate security software.
  • Windows Defender did not identify the modified SentinelOne DLL as malicious during the incident, despite its missing signature, added entry point, and encrypted payload embedded in its resources.
  • The article advises keeping Microsoft’s vulnerable driver blocklist current because known vulnerable drivers are increasingly being used to disable endpoint protections.
Key Points
  • 01The INC ransomware affiliate gained initial access through a ClickFix-style attack that tricked a user into running a malicious PowerShell command after visiting pet-care-related websites.
  • 02After gaining access, the threat actor used credential harvesting, RDP login attempts, and pass-the-hash activity to move across the victim network.
  • 03Investigators found four distinct bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver toolkits across multiple hosts, including xhunter1.sys, BdApiUtil64.sys, havoc.sys, and a newly observed package using the IoDrv driver.
  • 04The novel "Redacted EDR Blinder" utility installed a vulnerable driver and attempted to disable functions in security products including Microsoft Defender, Field Effect Covalence, Kaspersky Endpoint Security, Bitdefender, Qihoo 360, and SentinelOne.
  • 05The attackers used a modified SentinelOne DLL with its signature removed and an encrypted payload embedded in its resources to conceal a backdoor that supported file downloads, firewall changes, and Wasabi cloud-storage-based data exfiltration.

Manchester Airports Group reportedly suffered a data-extortion breach affecting about 8.7 million customers after FulcrumSec allegedly used exposed Iterable API credentials in client-side JavaScript to steal 86 GB of data. Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates Manchester Airport, London Stansted Airport, and East Midlands Airport, reported a data breach on 25 August 2026. The incident reportedly affected personal information belonging to about 8.7 million customers, largely from airport Wi-Fi sign-ups, parking, lounge, and Fast Track security booking services. MAG temporarily suspended its online Manage My Booking service, while stating that passenger safety, aviation security, and flight operations continued normally.

FulcrumSec claimed the breach on 30 August and told BleepingComputer it had stolen about 86 GB of data. The group alleged that it accessed airport-specific Iterable API credentials exposed in client-side JavaScript and obtained nearly 200,000 records concerning travel planned for the rest of 2026. The article says that although payment-card information was not taken, information such as email addresses, phone numbers, postcodes, and vehicle registrations could be used for targeted email and text-message scams or identity fraud. It also highlights that separating customer-facing platforms from core operational systems limited disruption to airport operations.

  • Customer-facing services such as Wi-Fi portals, parking, lounge bookings, and Fast Track reservations can hold substantial personal data even when they are separate from core airport operations.
  • Segregating ancillary web platforms from aviation and operational systems allowed MAG to suspend its booking portal without disrupting flight operations, passenger safety, or aviation security.
  • The alleged exposure of Iterable API credentials in client-side JavaScript reflects a technique the article says FulcrumSec also used against Arup Group, making continuous reviews of web application code especially important.
  • MAG’s public guidance about what information was and was not taken may reduce fraud risk by warning customers before criminals use the data for scams.

    Summary
    GitLab’s non-expiring incoming-email token can act as a reusable credential: anyone who obtains a user’s project email address can submit patches that GitLab commits under that user’s permissions, potentially to main and with CI/CD execution.     Aikido Security reported that GitLab’s private incoming-email address for creating work items contains a non-expiring token tied to a user account. The token is reused across the user’s project addresses and can apply to every public or private project that the account can access. GitLab does not verify the email sender, so anyone who obtains the address can submit email that GitLab handles with the account owner’s permissions.

    By changing the address suffix from -issue to -merge-request, a holder can email an attached patch and specify a target branch in the subject line. GitLab can apply the patch as a commit authored by the account owner, including to main where that user has permission, and a changed .gitlab-ci.yml can trigger CI/CD jobs. Incoming email is exempt from IP restrictions and can work without two-factor authentication; users can reset their incoming-email token to invalidate addresses, while self-managed administrators can disable incoming email across the instance.

    • Although GitLab presents the address as belonging to a particular project, its embedded token applies to every public or private project that the account can access.
    • An address intended for emailing work items can be converted into a code-submission route simply by replacing its “-issue” suffix with “-merge-request.”
    • A private project is not fully reachable from the token alone: an attacker also needs the project path and numeric ID, while public projects expose both values.
    • GitLab changed its wording to acknowledge that the address can create merge requests, but the article says the non-expiring token, unverified senders, and lack of an individual opt-out remain unchanged.
    • Resetting the incoming-email token invalidates all of a user’s project email addresses at once, and self-managed GitLab offers only an instance-wide disable option rather than a per-user setting.

GitLab gives users special email addresses for adding work items to projects, but the article says anyone who gets one of these addresses can also add code, start automated build jobs, and act as that user in other projects they can access. This can affect GitLab.com accounts and self-managed GitLab servers with email-based work item creation enabled, including private projects that are supposed to be limited to certain network locations. The risk is that a publicly shared or leaked address could let someone secretly change software, steal private project information, or use automated jobs to access sensitive data, creating a supply-chain risk for people who use that software.

Summary
GitLab’s project “incoming email” addresses embed a long-lived, account-wide token that can be used by anyone who obtains it to create merge requests, push patches to branches including main, and trigger CI/CD across projects the owner can access. The email path also bypasses GitLab IP restrictions, so users should rotate these tokens and scan repositories and documentation for exposed addresses.

GitLab’s “Email work item to this project” feature provides an incoming email address containing a long-lived token tied to the user’s account. The article reports that this token is identical in addresses generated for different projects and can reach every project the account can access, rather than only the project displayed in the interface. GitLab processes messages sent from any sender address as the token owner, according to the article.

Changing an address suffix from -issue to -merge-request allows merge-request emails, and a Git patch attachment can modify a source branch, including adding a CI/CD job. The researchers report confirming that this path could push code to a protected branch in a private project and run jobs even when the project was protected by an IP allowlist that blocked their browser and Git access. GitLab updated UI wording and documentation after disclosure, but the article says users should rotate incoming email tokens, scan for exposed addresses, and not treat IP allowlists as absolute boundaries for email-based changes.

  • The token alone is not sufficient to target another private project: the attacker must also know that project’s path slug and ID, while public projects expose both values.

  • GitLab’s available reset control invalidates all of a user’s incoming-email addresses at once, and the article states there is no per-project disablement, sender-verification requirement, or bulk-revocation mechanism.

In plain words

Researchers found a Firefox add-on that pretends to verify a person’s identity before opening protected PDF files, but can secretly take over Google accounts after it is installed. It targets Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking users and can steal a logged-in account’s access information or change the account password without the victim knowing. Although it appears to have few users so far, it matters because it was designed to look harmless during review and only downloads its harmful instructions later, making this kind of scam harder to spot.

Summary
A malicious Firefox extension posing as a PDF identity verifier remotely arms itself after installation to inject scripts into real Google sign-in pages, steal OAuth session cookies, and potentially reset victims’ passwords. Organizations should remove pdf-para-texto@extensao.local, revoke affected Google sessions, reset credentials from clean devices, and block pdf.gusercontent.com.

Socket identified a malicious Firefox extension, pdf-para-texto@extensao.local, that posed as a PDF identity-verification tool and was published to the Firefox Add-ons store on September 3, 2026. Its malicious functionality was introduced in version 1.4 on September 11, 2026, targeting Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking users. The extension had no significant user base at publication, but Socket highlighted its design to avoid detection by shipping without hardcoded malicious code, target URLs, or theft endpoints.

After installation, the extension opened an attacker-controlled lookalike domain, pdf.gusercontent.com, which delivered configuration and a payload through an open message bridge. Once armed, it watched Google responses for oauth_token cookies, sent captured values to an attacker endpoint, and injected a script into real accounts.google.com pages. The injected script hid its activity behind a fake identity-validation overlay, automated Google’s sign-in flow, and could silently set a new password when Google prompted for a password reset, giving the attacker both session access and potentially attacker-controlled credentials.

  • The extension was designed so that store review and static scanning would see a generic, apparently harmless dispatcher rather than hardcoded malicious URLs, credential theft logic, or payload code.
  • A page opened automatically after installation could send messages through an exposed bridge and direct the extension’s privileged background component to save attacker-supplied settings, which then activated its monitoring and code-injection behavior.
  • The attackers had two concurrent routes to access an account: capturing an OAuth session cookie from Google responses and, when Google required it, silently setting a new password controlled by the attackers.
  • The injected script ran on Google’s real account pages and used a full-screen “Validating your identity…” overlay to conceal the automated account-takeover process from the victim.
Key Points
  • 01Socket identified a malicious Firefox extension, pdf-para-texto@extensao.local, that impersonates a PDF identity-verification utility and targets Google accounts.
  • 02The extension initially contains no hardcoded credential-stealing code or attacker addresses, instead retrieving its configuration and payload from attacker-controlled infrastructure after installation.
  • 03After being armed, the extension injects a script into real accounts.google.com pages, displays a fake identity-validation overlay, and automates parts of Google’s sign-in and recovery flows.
  • 04The extension monitors Google responses for Set-Cookie headers containing oauth_token and sends captured cookie values to the attacker’s collection endpoint.
  • 05Socket said the extension had no significant user base at publication, but its post-install payload delivery design makes detection more difficult.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete malicious Firefox extension campaign capable of stealing Google session cookies and potentially changing victims’ passwords. Group-IB reports that the RemControl Android banking trojan is being distributed through fake TVTap Google Play pages and malvertising campaigns targeting users in Europe, Canada, and the Middle East. Once granted Accessibility permissions, it can overlay banking apps, steal credentials, remotely control devices, and evade Google Play Protect by blocking its traffic.

Group-IB has identified RemControl, a new Android malware-as-a-service platform distributed through malvertising campaigns and fake Google Play pages impersonating the TVTap IPTV app. The first samples appeared in July, although associated infrastructure has been active since at least May. The malware targets users in Italy, France, Spain, Poland, Portugal, Canada, and countries in the Middle East. Researchers found more than 30 fake banking-app screens designed to steal banking credentials.

After obtaining Accessibility Service permission, RemControl can display full-screen fake screens over legitimate banking apps, capture PINs, banking codes, card expiry dates, and credentials, and remotely perform actions on the device. It can stream screenshots and interface data in real time, record user input, capture pattern-lock coordinates on multiple Android device brands, and make removal more difficult by exiting when certain settings pages are opened. The dropper also starts a VPN service that blocks Google Play services traffic, hindering Play Protect real-time checks, while encrypted control-server details are retrieved through Telegram channels to support infrastructure changes. Group-IB tracks the operator as UNKK based on a shared identifier, found Russian language in some overlay files, and suspects a possible connection to the Medusa banking trojan.

  • RemControl uses a VPN service to block Google Play services traffic, which prevents Play Protect from conducting real-time checks against known malicious apps.
  • The malware obtains encrypted control-server information through Telegram channels, allowing its operators to change their infrastructure if it is disrupted.
  • RemControl can detect when a victim opens app-management, accessibility, or factory-reset settings and automatically exit to make removal more difficult.
  • The fake download sites contain Meta Pixel tracking IDs, which Group-IB says suggests the operators used Meta’s advertising ecosystem to direct people to the malicious pages.
  • One phishing screen displays an AI assistant response, which Group-IB identifies as a strong indication that AI models helped create the malware.

In plain words

Researchers found a Windows program called AvisLoader that tricks people with fake document-signing pages into copying and running a command on their own computer. Once installed, it can receive instructions and additional files through an encrypted peer-to-peer messaging network, making it harder to shut down by blocking a single website or server. People who fall for these fake verification requests may have their computers controlled by criminals, while organizations can look for suspicious copied commands, changed shortcuts, and unusual network activity to limit the damage.

Summary
Varonis researchers uncovered AvisLoader, a Windows malware loader delivered through ClickFix lures that uses the encrypted Tox peer-to-peer network for resilient command-and-control. Its shortcut-based persistence, optional UAC-bypass helper, and process-hiding DLL give defenders multiple host and network detection opportunities.

Varonis Threat Labs discovered AvisLoader, a Windows loader found on an exposed staging server alongside a ClickFix lure, supporting tools, and its Command Center. The lure impersonates a DocuSign signing request and tells visitors to copy and run a purported verification command that retrieves code from a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel address. Although the page displayed a macOS command, the recovered files included a Windows loader and no matching macOS payload.

AvisLoader uses the encrypted Tox peer-to-peer messaging network for operator commands and additional payloads, rather than depending on a fixed command-and-control domain or server address. Recovered artifacts indicate that it can modify desktop and taskbar shortcuts for persistence, and its bundled tools include a UAC-bypass helper and a library that can hide a specified process from software querying process information. The Command Center supports viewing client details, preparing shell commands for selected systems, and staging files for delivery over Tox; defenders can monitor suspicious copied commands, shortcut changes, and unexpected Tox traffic.

  • AvisLoader’s use of Tox means operators can move their controller by copying its Tox save file while clients retain the same peer identity, reducing dependence on a fixed domain or server address.
  • Although the fake verification page displayed a macOS command, the recovered staging directory contained a Windows loader and no corresponding macOS payload.
  • The loader contains seventeen same-sized, non-executable sections named after well-known packers, apparently to confuse identification rather than demonstrate that those packers were used.
  • Because victims paste the command themselves, the resulting activity may not show the browser as the parent process, making command-shell and script-interpreter monitoring especially useful.
  • The recovered UAC-bypass helper and process-hiding DLL show available capabilities, but the article does not establish that elevation succeeded or that the hiding DLL was deployed.
Key Points
  • 01AvisLoader is a 64-bit Windows loader discovered on an exposed staging server alongside a ClickFix lure, supporting tools, and its command center.
  • 02The ClickFix lure impersonates a DocuSign signing request and instructs visitors to copy and run a command that retrieves code from a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel address.
  • 03AvisLoader statically links c-toxcore and uses the encrypted Tox peer-to-peer network to receive commands and additional payloads without relying on a fixed command-and-control domain.
  • 04Recovered AvisLoader artifacts indicate shortcut-based persistence, include an auto.exe helper referencing a UACME UAC-bypass method, and include hmn_hook.dll, which can filter a process name from process-information results.
  • 05The AvisLoader Command Center supports managing clients, scheduling shell commands for matching clients that come online, and staging files for delivery over Tox.

In plain words

A website name often used as a harmless stand-in in developer examples, third-party.com, now shows a fake Cloudflare check to Windows visitors. It tells people to copy and run a command that can download and start unwanted software on their computer. This matters because developers may have copied the name into websites, apps, or test tools, which could lead people or automated software to an attacker-controlled page; unlike example.com, this domain was never protected for safe documentation use.

Summary
The commonly used but unreserved placeholder domain third-party.com is serving a fake Cloudflare verification page that tricks Windows users into pasting and running a malicious PowerShell command. Developers should replace literal references to the domain with IANA-reserved example domains, as copied documentation or test code could direct users to attacker-controlled content.

The domain third-party.com, long used as a placeholder in developer documentation, is serving a fake Cloudflare verification page to Windows users. The page uses a ClickFix scheme: after a visitor clicks its verification box, it copies a PowerShell command to the clipboard and instructs the visitor to open Windows Run, paste the command, and execute it. Manifold Security first reported the behavior after finding references to the domain in public AI skills and MCP server documentation, and BleepingComputer confirmed the fake CAPTCHA page.

The command reconstructs a payload URL, downloads a PowerShell script, and runs it. A May 2026 Hybrid Analysis report showed that the script previously downloaded a 134MB ZIP archive, extracted it, and attempted to launch draw.io.exe, although the archive was unavailable for further analysis and the payload host no longer resolved during testing. The campaign selectively targets Windows users; macOS and Linux visitors instead receive an unsupported-system message.

The incident is notable because third-party.com is not reserved for documentation, unlike IANA-maintained example.com, example.net, and example.org. The domain appears in more than 1,500 files across over 1,700 repositories and is used in some examples that could make real network requests if copied literally. There are no reports that these references have led to ClickFix execution on developers’ devices or in applications, but the live domain could be switched to another active payload source.

  • The malicious page delivers its command-copying behavior only to Windows users, while macOS and Linux visitors receive an unsupported-system message, making a casual review from those systems less likely to reveal the harmful behavior.

Microsoft says that September 2026 Windows 11 updates can prevent some computers from automatically connecting to their organization’s private network over the internet. The problem affects organizations using Always On VPN with an automatic fallback between two connection methods, leaving devices stuck trying to connect or showing a port error. Summary
Microsoft says September 2026 Windows 11 security updates can cause Always On VPN connections using automatic IKEv2/SSTP protocol fallback to hang or fail with a port-in-use error. Until a permanent fix is available, administrators should configure affected VPN profiles to use either IKEv2-only or SSTP-only.

Microsoft has warned that September 2026 Windows 11 security updates can cause Always On VPN connection problems for users trying to reach their organization’s enterprise network. Always On VPN automatically establishes a secure connection to a corporate network when a device connects to the internet and supports IKEv2 and SSTP connection protocols. Microsoft lists Windows 11 versions 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2 as affected, through KB5124012 and KB5124008.

The problem occurs when an Always On VPN profile is configured to automatically try another connection method after the initial method fails, such as switching between IKEv2 and SSTP. Affected connections may remain stuck in a “Connecting” state, repeatedly attempt to connect unsuccessfully, or later show the error, “The specified port is already in use.” While it works on a permanent fix, Microsoft advises IT administrators to configure affected profiles to use one protocol only—either SSTP or IKEv2—based on organizational requirements.

  • The affected configuration is specifically automatic protocol fallback, meaning organizations using a single Always On VPN protocol can avoid the documented failure mode without removing the service entirely.
  • Microsoft’s interim mitigation requires an operational trade-off: administrators must choose either SSTP or IKEv2 based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements while the permanent fix is pending.
  • The VPN issue is part of a broader set of September 2026 update problems that also prompted emergency fixes for Hyper-V, Remote Desktop Services, and USB audio issues.
  • The documented symptoms include both persistent connection attempts and a misleading-looking port-in-use error on later attempts, which can help distinguish this issue from a simple loss of network access.
