In plain words

A person using the name TheHatman offered millions of employee records said to come from nine major organizations, including names, work email addresses, job titles, phone numbers, managers, and administrator accounts. The records appear genuine, but it is unclear whether they came from recent break-ins, old data being resold, a shared outside service, or stolen employee logins. Even without passwords or customer information, these details can help criminals convincingly impersonate coworkers or IT staff and trick people into giving up access. The case shows that companies need to limit how much internal directory information any one employee, automated account, or AI tool can see and watch for unusual mass collection of it.

Summary
Alleged theft of 3.6 million Azure/Entra employee-directory records shows that even without passwords or customer data, organizational details can enable highly targeted phishing and identity attacks. Organizations should limit directory-read access, review Microsoft Graph and application permissions, and monitor for bulk directory enumeration.

In August 2026, a threat actor called TheHatman advertised roughly 3.6 million employee records attributed to nine major organizations, claiming they were obtained from Microsoft Azure and Entra environments. Cyera Research found that sampled data appeared genuine and included names, work email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, office locations, group memberships, service accounts, and privileged accounts. However, the evidence does not establish when the data was collected, where it originated, or whether TheHatman personally compromised the organizations named in the listings.

Several named organizations disputed recent breaches, with Tata Consultancy Services saying the material appeared more than four years old, Gap finding no evidence of a compromise, and Vodafone describing it as address-list or business-card-like information. The article notes that authentic records may be old data resold on underground markets, could stem from a shared third party or highly permitted application, or may involve compromised credentials, although no public analysis links a specific stolen credential to a listed directory export. Even without passwords or customer data, organizational directories can help criminals craft targeted phishing, executive impersonation, and account-recovery scams by revealing reporting lines, IT staff, service accounts, and administrator identities.

The article argues that organizations should assess what data a compromised employee, application, service account, or AI agent can access, rather than focusing only on preventing initial account compromise. Recommended measures include reducing unnecessary directory visibility, reviewing Microsoft Graph directory-read permissions, limiting standing administrator privileges, and watching for bulk user enumeration, unusual Graph requests, unexpected application consent, and unexpected directory exports. It also warns that help desks should not treat knowledge of internal employee details as proof of identity, since such information may already be available to attackers.

  • The usefulness of stolen directory data does not depend on it being current: genuine but older records can still provide organizational details that support convincing impersonation and phishing.
  • A single application, integration, or service account with broad directory-reading permission could potentially expose information across a cloud environment without requiring separate break-ins at every named organization.
  • Knowledge of an employee’s manager, department, title, phone number, or administrator should not be treated as reliable proof of identity in help-desk or account-recovery processes because such details may be available to attackers.
  • AI agents may create a broader and less predictable exposure than traditional service accounts because they can hold persistent access to multiple applications, APIs, databases, and cloud resources.
  • Security teams can look for potential directory theft by monitoring for unusually high Microsoft Graph requests, bulk user lookups by one identity, unexpected application consent, or unexpected directory exports.

In plain words

Researchers at Cisco Talos found a Windows malware program called CLOSEDQUORUM that is designed to ask several AI services to vote on what harmful step to take next, rather than waiting for an attacker to send direct instructions. If fully working, it could steal computer login details, saved web-browser passwords, and cryptocurrency wallet information, then send them to the attacker through Discord. The public sample does not work because it contains placeholder access codes, but it shows criminals are experimenting with AI to make malicious programs act more independently. This matters because people and organizations using Windows could face threats that are harder to recognize when a program combines AI-service connections with data theft and hidden ways to restart itself.

Summary
Cisco Talos identified CLOSEDQUORUM, an early Windows malware prototype that asks up to four commercial AI models to vote on post-compromise actions such as credential theft, persistence, and code injection. The publicly available sample is nonfunctional, but its design shows attackers experimenting with AI services as a substitute for traditional command-and-control.

Cisco Talos reported on CLOSEDQUORUM, a Windows malware prototype designed to ask up to four commercial AI services—DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini—to vote on what it should do next. Rather than receiving direct commands from an attacker-controlled server, it sends the models basic information about a computer and a fixed menu of actions. Talos said it is the first publicly documented Windows implant, to its knowledge, that delegates command-and-control decisions to AI models. The public version does not function as published because it contains placeholder API keys and Discord webhook details.

The available actions are steal, inject, persist, and move, although the move option has no implementation in the public version. A steal decision can trigger Windows credential-memory dumping, collection of saved browser passwords, and theft of data from MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum wallets; other options can inject code into programs or create several automatic-start mechanisms. The malware sends the models’ choices and stated reasons to an attacker Discord channel before acting, and sends stolen data there in encrypted pieces. Talos advised defenders to detect suspicious combinations of AI-service traffic, LSASS access, process injection, persistence activity, and Discord webhook connections rather than blocking AI-service domains alone.

  • CLOSEDQUORUM does not simply use AI to generate commands; it gives the models a fixed menu of actions and performs whichever action receives the most valid votes.
  • The malware sends both its decisions and the models' stated reasons to a Discord channel before acting, giving an attacker visibility without operating a traditional command server.
  • Its reliance on commercial AI services creates operational weaknesses because providers can refuse requests, rate-limit them, or return unusable responses.
  • Blocking AI-service domains alone would be unreliable because legitimate software may use those services; Talos recommends detecting the combination of AI requests with credential access, code injection, persistence, and Discord traffic instead.
Key Points
  • 01Cisco Talos reported that CLOSEDQUORUM is a Windows malware prototype designed to ask up to four commercial AI models—DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini—to vote on its next action.
  • 02The malware can choose among stealing data, injecting code into another program, establishing automatic restart mechanisms, or moving laterally, although the public version has no code for the move option.
  • 03When the steal action is selected, CLOSEDQUORUM attempts to collect Windows login credentials, saved passwords from Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and data from MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum cryptocurrency wallets.
  • 04The public sample contains placeholder AI-service API keys and Discord webhook values, so it cannot contact the models or send stolen data as published.
  • 05Talos advised defenders to look for an unusual combination of AI-service traffic, access to Windows credential memory, process injection or persistence activity, and Discord webhook traffic.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he has ordered security chiefs to begin work on a National Centre for Information Defence to detect, attribute and disrupt hostile state disinformation. The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s first reporting deadline is now active, requiring companies to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents involving products with digital elements within 24 hours of becoming aware of them. Reports are submitted through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform, followed by a 72-hour notification with threat and mitigation details. For exploited vulnerabilities, the final report is due 14 days after remediation is delivered; for severe incidents, it is due one month after the 72-hour notification.

The reporting obligation does not apply to every vulnerability a company finds, only those actively exploited with malicious intent or severe incidents affecting product security. Companies must also inform affected users about corrective measures, but do not need to pre-register with the platform before having something to report. In plain words

The article describes a design risk in Google’s system for letting developers request cloud changes through Kubernetes configuration files instead of giving them direct cloud login keys. If the system’s own account has very broad control over a company’s Google Cloud organization, someone who can submit certain files in a Kubernetes workspace may be able to grant themselves full control of that organization. This affects organizations using Google Kubernetes Config Connector with overly powerful accounts and loose access rules, because a small amount of cluster access could lead to control of cloud data, services, and permissions.

Summary
Google Kubernetes Config Connector can become a privilege-escalation path when its shared service account has broad Google Cloud IAM permissions and namespace users can create IAM policy resources. An attacker could then submit a single Kubernetes YAML manifest to grant themselves organization-level ownership without possessing Google Cloud credentials.

Google Kubernetes Config Connector (KCC) lets developers request Google Cloud resources through Kubernetes YAML files while KCC uses its own Google service account to make cloud API calls. Researcher Justin O’Leary identified a technique called ConfigConfusion, in which a user with permission to create IAMPolicyMember resources in a KCC-managed namespace can indirectly use KCC’s cloud permissions. If KCC’s service account has organization-level authority, the user can submit a YAML file that grants an attacker roles/owner for the entire Google Cloud organization without needing Google Cloud credentials.

The issue stems from two separate authorization systems: Kubernetes checks whether the user may create the resource in the namespace, while Google Cloud checks only whether KCC’s service account may make the requested change. Google Cloud therefore sees KCC rather than the Kubernetes user who initiated the request, creating a confused deputy problem. Google describes KCC as working as designed and recommends reducing KCC’s IAM authority, using separately scoped accounts where possible, restricting access to IAM-related KCC resources, and monitoring organization- and folder-level IAM changes made by KCC.

  • The risk arises from the combination of two separately reasonable decisions: granting KCC broad Google Cloud permissions and allowing developers to create IAM-related Kubernetes resources.
  • Google considers this behavior to be working as designed, making configuration review rather than a software patch the primary response described in the article.
  • The credential-free model can obscure accountability because Google Cloud records KCC’s service account as making the change rather than the Kubernetes user who requested it.
  • AWS Controllers for Kubernetes and Azure Service Operator v2 reduce potential impact by separating controller permissions by service or namespace, although they do not remove the underlying authorization gap.
  • A practical mitigation is to treat permission to create IAMPolicyMember, IAMPolicy, and IAMPartialPolicy resources as highly privileged Kubernetes access.
Key Points
  • 01Google Kubernetes Config Connector lets developers declare Google Cloud resources in Kubernetes YAML files while the controller authenticates to Google Cloud using its own service account.
  • 02The ConfigConfusion technique can let a user who can create IAMPolicyMember resources in a KCC-managed namespace use KCC's Google Cloud permissions indirectly.
  • 03If KCC's service account can assign organization-level roles, a malicious YAML resource can grant an attacker roles/owner over the Google Cloud organization without the attacker having Google Cloud credentials.
  • 04Kubernetes RBAC checks whether a user may create a resource in the cluster, while Google Cloud IAM sees only KCC's service account when it performs the requested cloud change.
  • 05Google recommends limiting KCC service-account permissions and restricting who can create IAMPolicyMember, IAMPolicy, and IAMPartialPolicy resources.

In plain words

A new security report says criminals and state-backed hackers are increasingly breaking into the central control panels that businesses use to manage their network equipment. Serious flaws in products from Cisco, SonicWall, Check Point, and others can let an outsider take control without a password, steal account details, or install ransomware that locks company files. This matters because one compromised management system can give attackers a path into many devices at once, making the damage much wider than a problem with a single computer.

Summary
Eclypsium warns that attackers are increasingly exploiting network-management platforms, where a single compromise can provide control over entire enterprise infrastructure. The report highlights actively exploited critical flaws in Cisco FMC and ISE, SonicWall SMA 1000, and other infrastructure products, urging rapid patching, monitoring, and hardening.

Eclypsium’s September InfraTrust Pulse reports that attackers are increasingly targeting the management systems used to configure and control enterprise infrastructure. Between August 25 and September 17, the report tracked 158 advisories from 17 vendors covering 1,699 vulnerabilities, including 42 rated critical and 71 remotely exploitable without authentication. Five advisories included flaws later added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Eclypsium says management platforms should be treated as high-value targets because they hold credentials and can control many devices at once.

The report highlights actively exploited Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center and Identity Services Engine flaws, including CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-76460, which can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root. Cisco Talos linked attacks chaining two FMC flaws to three threat clusters, with attackers using built-in tools for reconnaissance, harvesting credentials, deploying tunneling utilities, and in some cases deploying Qilin ransomware. InfraTrust also cited actively exploited SonicWall SMA 1000 flaws that can be chained for unauthenticated remote code execution, as well as critical Check Point, Arista, and Cisco Nexus issues. The report further noted that the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431, known as CopyFail, appears in 19 advisories from six vendors, creating separate remediation tasks across vendor schedules.

  • The most consequential flaws are increasingly appearing in management consoles rather than the network devices themselves, meaning one compromised console can expose credentials and change-control access across many devices.
  • Cisco's FMC attacks involved chaining CVE-2026-20079 with CVE-2026-20316, and Cisco had published an indicator of compromise associated with both flaws before it confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-20079.
  • For the actively exploited SonicWall SMA 1000 flaws, SonicWall recommends re-imaging physical appliances or redeploying virtual appliances instead of trying to clean compromised systems in place.
  • A single Linux kernel flaw, CVE-2026-31431, generated 19 separate remediation tasks across six vendors, illustrating how vendor-specific advisory schedules complicate patching for shared components.
Key Points
  • 01Eclypsium's September InfraTrust Pulse tracked 158 new security advisories across 17 vendors, covering 1,699 vulnerabilities between August 25 and September 17.
  • 02The report says attackers are increasingly targeting infrastructure management platforms, which can provide control over many network devices and their credentials at once.
  • 03Cisco confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-20079, an authentication bypass in Secure Firewall Management Center that can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root.
  • 04Cisco Talos linked attacks chaining two Cisco FMC vulnerabilities to threat clusters UAT-12197, UAT-11823, and UAT-11988, with some incidents involving Qilin ransomware.
  • 05InfraTrust found that the Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw CVE-2026-31431, known as CopyFail, appears in 19 advisories from six vendors.

In plain words

CTF.ae has introduced XRanges for AI, a service that tests automated security programs against realistic practice companies and records what they actually do. It checks whether the programs explored the company, found problems for real, followed the rules, and avoided damaging the test environment. This matters to teams building these tools because an automated program’s written report can be wrong or incomplete, while checking every claim by hand takes substantial expert time.

Summary
CTF.ae is promoting XRanges for AI, a platform that evaluates autonomous security agents on instrumented, realistic targets using coverage, boundary compliance, verified exploit progress, and environment integrity scores. The company says the system was stress-tested across hundreds of isolated deployments during DEF CON 34’s Bug Bounty Village CTF.

CTF.ae presents XRanges for AI as a platform for evaluating autonomous security agents against realistic, isolated multi-service applications. The platform is designed to address the difficulty of determining whether an agent genuinely found and exploited a flaw, merely encountered a clue, or invented a finding in its own report. It also aims to reduce the expert review burden created by testing multiple models, prompts, and repeated runs.

Each target includes application-specific OpenTelemetry instrumentation and 20 or more injected vulnerabilities, including multi-step chains across services. XRanges for AI scores deployments on coverage of normal business actions, compliance with rules of engagement, verified progress through exploitation steps, and the target’s continued functional integrity. CTF.ae says the same monitoring approach was used during the 48-hour DEF CON 34 Bug Bounty Village CTF, where it observed more than 850 deployments for 545 registered players.

  • An agent’s report alone cannot distinguish a confirmed exploit from a partial attempt or an invented claim, so XRanges for AI verifies activity from inside the target rather than relying on the agent’s narrative.
  • The platform treats unvisited normal features as explicit blind spots, which can reveal what an agent never attempted rather than only rewarding the issues it reported.
  • A reported issue absent from the target’s known vulnerability list can be checked against the recorded activity, allowing the platform to separate false positives from previously unplanned real bugs.
  • The same deployment can be patched or have vulnerabilities disabled for retesting, preserving the target’s state instead of requiring a newly built test environment.
  • The DEF CON deployment monitoring was intended to validate whether players reached findings through legitimate paths and to identify unintended shortcuts such as outside CVEs or container escapes.
Key Points
  • 01CTF.ae’s XRanges for AI evaluates autonomous security agents against isolated, multi-service benchmark applications that contain 20 or more injected vulnerabilities.
  • 02The platform uses application-level telemetry to measure four signals during each run: coverage of normal business functions, rule-boundary violations, verified progress through vulnerability exploitation steps, and target integrity.
  • 03XRanges for AI lets teams inspect an agent’s activity timeline, query raw OpenTelemetry data, and compare repeated runs using metadata such as model, agent version, and prompt variant.
  • 04Targets can be patched or have vulnerabilities toggled in place so agents can retest in the same environment and state.
  • 05CTF.ae says it used the underlying instrumentation across more than 850 deployments during the 48-hour DEF CON 34 Bug Bounty Village CTF, involving 545 registered players.

attachments concept

audit concept

Automation concept
Automation uses software to perform tasks with little or no human intervention.

belgium other

binary concept

bitcoin

bitdefender organization

breach concept

breached concept

china

chinadigitaltimes[.]top other

cluster concept

coding concept
